item.title: Why Am I So Angry All the Time? Practical Tips to Overcome Anger
item.description:
The Heart Angle

It is important to discuss anger from a heartfelt perspective, although anger is not known for being a heartfelt emotion. When a person asks why they are so angry all the time, the root cause may not be known, so the question will only be partially answered.

The root cause for a great deal of the anger that is experienced derives from issues or matters of the heart. There is a saying that says there is a thin line between love and hate. Indeed, it is so thin that at times their distance from one another is small.

As a therapist, I have found that when anger is unpacked, it often stems from heartbreak caused by disappointment, loss, grief, lack of progress, feelings of failure, rejection, abandonment, and even a lack of felt love. Anger is often telling you what you are avoiding.

Emotions are the byproduct of the deeper symptoms. What is going on in your heart that is portraying itself as anger? To answer this question, we must go underneath. Your anger is trying to tell you something. The question is: what? This is often what is occurring.

  • There is hurt without clarity.
  • Undealt-with rejection.
  • Unhealed abandonment.
  • You may be feeling powerless.
  • You may be feeling ignored.
  • You may have tolerated something for too long.
  • You may be feeling stuck.
  • You may even be angry because there is a truth somewhere in your life that you have been unwilling or unable to confront.

Take the time to consider each thought. Allow it to sit with you.

Anger and Our Relationship with the Truth

I believe a great deal of anger can be connected to our relationship with truth. Sometimes we are angry because we cannot tell the truth. Sometimes we are angry because we do not want to face the truth. Sometimes we are angry because we are not living according to what we know is true.

Then there are times when we are angry because someone else told us the truth and we were not ready to hear it. The truth can be uncomfortable. Truth can seem threatening. Truth can even seem insulting without the intention of being so.

Maybe you continue saying yes to people when you really want to push back. Yet the deeper problem may not be that people keep asking. The deeper problem may be that you have not been honest about what you can handle. You have trouble admitting your limitations, and you would rather die than have anyone perceive a weakness.

Perhaps you are angry about your lack of professional progression. You are feeling overlooked by your superiors and undervalued. You resent your coworkers for getting what you deserve. You used to love your company and once saw a future there. But now you dread work mornings. Deep down, you know it is time to make a change, but fear has prevented you from making a change.

Truth will also require you to acknowledge when you have participated in your own frustration. There are times when we remain in situations long after we know something must change. Nevertheless, we become angry with people for crossing boundaries we have never verbalized or enforced.

We may even become irritated when others do not recognize needs that we have never expressed. Standing toe to toe with truth means asking yourself what part of the situation belongs to you. That moment may be uncomfortable, but it can help show us where we still have the power to move differently.

Your anger is real. But so is the hurtful and hard-to-face truth underneath it. Jesus said that the truth would make us free. Freedom has never begun with pretending. Freedom requires us to become willing to see what is there. Sometimes anger increases because we are fighting reality that we feel helpless to change.

Think About It, You May Not Be Angry About Today

A major reason why anger can feel disproportionate is that the current situation is carrying the weight of several previous situations. Someone does something tiny, and in return you respond enormously. Ever wonder when you became so upset? The other person may wonder the same thing.

The answer could be that you were not only responding to what happened today, because that is all you can see in the moment. However, you neglected to really comprehend that you were responding to every time you felt overlooked. Not to mention every time you were disappointed, or for each time a promise was broken, or for each conversation that went unresolved.

Think about it, you may not be angry about today, but for every moment you have decided not to say anything. Your anger had been accumulating when experiences that you had in your life were not properly processed. This is why it is not unusual to encounter some people going from zero to one hundred over something that appears insignificant.

The current situation may simply be the final place where everything else came to a head. In those intense moments, ask yourself, “What else am I responding to right now?” The answer could separate today’s frustration from yesterday’s wound.

Practical Tips to Overcome Anger

The goal of overcoming anger is not to become a person who never gets angry. This is unrealistic and not maintainable. The key to overcoming anger is learning how to recognize what your anger is revealing before it begins attempting to take center stage. Your anger becomes more manageable when you have practical steps that can help you move from reacting to your anger toward understanding it and responding differently.

Identify what is happening beneath the anger Instead of “I am upset,” finish the sentence: “I am angry because I felt…” Permit yourself to go above and beyond what may have been your obvious answer. Were you feeling ashamed? Did you feel disregarded? Did you feel powerless? Remember, naming what is at the root of your anger will aid you in understanding what really needs your attention,

Start separating what you can change from what you cannot control Ask: “What am I avoiding?” You may already know what needs to be changed. The hard part may be accepting what that truth may require from us.

Do not shut down speaking what you feel sooner Do not make silence carry something until anger has to announce it. You cannot control another person’s choices. You can control what you participate in. You can decide what you will tolerate. You can also determine what access someone will continue to have to you.

Examine your expectations Determine what was conveyed. Do not make silence carry something until anger has to announce it. Learn to communicate frustration while it is still frustration. Not everything requires confrontation, but important matters should not continually be buried.

Decide what you should be grieving instead of correcting Some things cannot be fixed. They must be mourned. Some things cannot be fixed. They must be mourned. You may be trying to get an apology you will never receive or attempting to change something that has already happened. Grief may be necessary where correction is no longer possible.

Choose what your anger will yield Let it lead to a boundary, conversation, decision, healing work, or change rather than damage. Anger has energy attached to it. Decide where that energy will go. Your anger can destroy something or reveal what needs to be different. The responsibility is deciding what happens next.

item.title: How Social Media Algorithms Can Affect Self-Esteem
item.description:
In the modern age of technology, social media platforms have become not only a means of communication/connection but a way of seeking psychological comfort. Various social media platforms such as TikTok, Instagram, Meta, and YouTube use algorithms to assess your perceived interests and continue showing feeds of those interests.

But what exactly is an algorithm, and can it change? What is the connection between these algorithms and one’s interpretation of self-esteem? Who is mostly impacted by this occurrence? This article will focus on these primary questions, outcomes, and alternatives to address a growing concern of social media use among America’s youth.

Algorithms

Per the Merriam-Webster dictionary, an algorithm is “a step-by-step set of instructions or rules used to solve a problem, perform a calculation, or complete a specific task.” Simply put, different platforms, including social media, use algorithms to target content that is perceived to be preferred by the person using various feeds on social media.

The algorithms on social media are set by the duration of a video watched. For example, if a person scrolls past several videos but watches a video for thirty seconds or more, an algorithm is created to show you more videos of similar content.

For instance, if you enjoy watching videos of people doing do-it-yourself (DIY) projects and watch various DIY videos, the algorithm will show you predominantly DIY videos. These algorithms are typically broken when a new algorithm is created based on a perceived change of interest, or you spend more time on different feeds. On most social media platforms, you can have more than one algorithm depending on your interests.

Connection of Algorithms and Self-Esteem

Now that we know what an algorithm is and how it works, what impact does it have on one’s self-esteem? Think of a particular feed that may touch an insecurity of yours. For example, maybe you are having a rather difficult time in life, and you see more videos of people demonstrating happiness, wealth, etc., and now these videos cause a psychological reaction.

This can be as simple as “I was already having a horrible day because of work, now I see other people happy at their jobs on TikTok, and I feel worse now about my situation.” For many adults, compared to adolescents/teenagers, social media may serve as a temporary or even regular outlet to disconnect from day-to-day stressors.

However, these algorithms pose a risk of developing a sense of dependence on them to relieve stress, anxiety, or bring happiness (e.g., laughter from videos you find hilarious). Therefore, there are potentially consequential implications of this depending on the algorithms you have and the frequency of your social media use.

Who is impacted or how is someone affected?

Social media has different impacts on different age groups. First, let’s look at the social and psychological impacts on American youth. One of the largest concerns is the prevalence of cyberbullying, and leading to riskier behaviors among youth.

According to Khalaf, et. al. (2023), American youth who are overly exposed to social media, particularly in late adolescence and teenage years, are at higher risk of developing psychopathology such as clinical depression, anxiety and/or phobia disorders, and suicidal ideation.

Per their study, researchers found that 14.8% of adolescent psychiatric admissions to hospitals between 2016 and 2020 reported that the primary reason for their admission was due to cyberbullying on social media, which led to them feeling overwhelming suicidal ideation (Khalaf, et. al., 2023).

This research study also found a significant correlation between before and/or during bedtime use of social media/technology and poorer sleep and eventual academic decline. Additional concerns consist of unmonitored activities on social media platforms that depict pseudo pornographic content.

This has resulted in a high prevalence among adolescents and teenagers using pornography, which can cause several other psychological and physiological challenges. Positive uses of social media include better awareness of the importance of taking care of one’s mental health, humor content, identity formation, and creative expression.

Now let’s compare this to adults. Similar to youth, social media serves as a multi-purposed outlet for everyday life. However, the risks are different and often more damaging compared to youth. For instance, employers in the last ten years have used social media posts of their employees as justifications for terminating their employment.

In addition, with vast amounts of knowledge on social media, threats of violence have exponentially increased, including threats to find where people live, work, or where their children go to school. According to Naslund, et. al. (2020), an estimated 3.8 billion people in the world had access to social media in 2020, which included a large demographic of adults living with mental illnesses.

This exposed adults with and without serious mental illnesses to influences that challenge or question one’s reality. For example, with the various conspiracy theories circulating on social media, adults who live with conditions like schizophrenia are more prone to having their existing symptoms become more severe (Naslund, et. al., 2020).

Additionally, social media use has significantly impacted in-person social interactions. Following the COVID-19 pandemic, many adults found that a temporary method of communication (i.e., due to government isolation regulations) never reverted to previous methods of communication.

This includes fewer social interactions and difficulty handling social conflicts in an appropriate manner. This became even more prevalent when social media trends such as recording altercations became popular as a form of entertainment and with a disregard for law, order, or civility. In fact, these social media trends have gained such popularity that certain platforms pay you to watch them, which triggers more algorithms.

What is the impact of social media on Christianity?

Social media has had a two-fold impact on Christianity. On one side, Christianity continues to be vilified as a hateful religion that ostracizes anyone who does not think, feel, or believe in every word of the Bible. For example, while at a Mariners game at T-Mobile Park in Seattle, you might see a group of people with signs saying that a certain demographic of people (often an explicit or vulgar adjective) “…are going to hell, repent now or be judged!”

This video and several others like it flood social media platforms and convince several people (youth and adults alike) that Christianity is a hateful religion. This is largely seen in major U.S. metropolitan cities across the country in universities, colleges, high schools, and public events. This not only makes it difficult to convince others of the good news of Jesus Christ, but it tarnishes its validity in their eyes.

The other side is a great promotion of Christianity. Specifically, having younger adults worshiping God influences other youth and even adults to give their lives over to God. Social media platforms in the last five years have even been used by churches across the United States to promote community events and overall advertisement of the church. However, depending on the algorithm, people can be influenced either positively or negatively.

What is a potential solution to harmful social media use?

Simple options include limiting social media use as an adult and really understanding your daily dependence on it. If you feel you cannot get off social media despite overt negative repercussions, seek professional help, as you may be demonstrating addictive-type behaviors.

Limit screen time for youth and have appropriate parental locks as needed. Parents should have regular conversations with their kids about social media use and make sure they are doing okay. Practice having more conversations in person and do not recklessly debate people on social media (especially people you do not know).

item.title: From Taboo to Therapy: The Journey of Gen X Mental Health Wellness
item.description:
Generation X represents people born between 1965 and 1980. It is a quiet generation between the idealism of baby boomers and the outspoken awareness of millennials. This is where the term “The Forgotten Generation” stems from. In the Gen X world, independence was prized, and emotional toughness was highly valued.

There were only whispered conversations about mental health, and often, the subject was dismissed entirely. For many individuals in Gen X, survival meant being silent about their emotional pain. Mental health wellness for Gen X is now transforming a generation that was once overlooked into one that recognizes and values mental well-being.

As this generation navigates midlife, they balance careers, families, aging parents, and their faith. And in the midst of this, they have discovered that the inner silence of their youth has come with consequences.

Many Gen X adults wrestle with anxiety, loneliness, or emotional exhaustion underneath their competence and calmness. “Keep it together” was the cultural message of their youth. But faith reminds them that God never intended for people to carry the weight of their hearts alone.

…For the Lord sees not as man sees: man looks on the outward appearance, but the Lord looks on the heart. – 1 Samuel 16:7, ESV

Growing Up Under the Weight of Mental Health Taboo

The Gen X story is often portrayed in terms of resilience. This generation is when latchkey kids became a household role. These kids came home to empty houses, heating leftovers in microwaves, and learning independence early. However, what was once labeled as self-reliance was sometimes masked as emotional neglect. Many in this generation were taught that strength meant silence.

Even in many church settings, culturally, the expressions of emotions were met with caution. Tears were for the weak, depression was something to pray about privately, and for those of faith, counseling was considered unnecessary.

Gen X learned to compartmentalize, separating emotions from spirituality and faith from vulnerability. The mental health and wellness of Gen X individuals focused on how well they could maintain their strength regardless of what was going on within themselves.

During this time, the church focused on behavior and doctrine, but hardly ever on emotional health. From the pulpit, Gen X was taught holiness in obedience. Trauma, anxiety, or need for emotional restoration was seldom addressed. Many Gen X believers grew to love God deeply, yet they struggled to believe that He cared about their inner pain.

Faith asks that we be honest about sin as well as sorrow. God delights in the truth regarding all of our being, even in the deepest places of our minds. This is an invitation that challenges the old taboo of silence and opens the door for authentic spiritual wellness for Gen X individuals.

The Hidden Struggles of Gen X

The individuals of Gen X have achieved a great deal when viewed from the outside. They are dependable, competent, and quite effective. But beneath that steadiness lies a generation that has carried more emotional weight than they were taught to manage.

This has resulted in many individuals living with the effects of chronic stress and suppressed emotions. Some battle depression or anxiety, and they hesitate to seek help because they have been taught they should handle it. Others carry unhealed childhood wounds, such as neglect, divorce, or instability.

In midlife, the unspoken burdens often surface, creating a need for relief from burdens they were never meant to carry. Balancing teenage children and aging parents creates emotional strain. Coupled with careers that once felt purposeful and friendships that are harder to maintain, GenX often experience a crisis of faith and wonder if God still sees them amid the demands of everyone else’s needs.

Christian counselors emphasize that Scripture reminds believers that God not only sees, but He also sustains. This doesn’t mean that emotions should be suppressed instead. It is an invitation to release it. They remind Gen X individuals that God understands emotions, and they don’t need to keep carrying weight that was never meant to be carried alone.

Cast your burden on the Lord, and he will sustain you; he will never permit the righteous to be moved. – Psalm 55:22, ESV

Faith and Feelings: A Revisited Tension

Many Gen X Christians feel as though emotional honesty is risky. During their youth, the church culture often defined faith as the solution to every struggle and left little room for lament or any open conversation regarding mental health. When faced with an overwhelming situation, they were often told to pray about it. This resulted in the ability to hide emotions, keep struggles a secret, and remain strong on the outside.

Prayer is powerful, but without acknowledgment of pain, it becomes another form of denial. Jesus modeled emotional transparency. He wept over Lazarus’s death. He grieved over Jerusalem and anguished in Gethsemane. Jesus did not hide his feelings. Still, a generation of emotional suppression can’t be dismantled when they read that Jesus wept.

These words affirm that tears are not an indicator of a lack of faith, but rather an expression of its fullness. These examples validate any emotional expression as part of spiritual life. For Gen X believers, this truth means rediscovering the heart of faith that integrates mind, soul, and emotion under God’s care.

From Stigma to Seeking Help: Mental Health Wellness for Gen X

Slowly, this generation is moving forward to seek help without shame. What was once seen as a weakness is now recognized as a tool for healing. Gen X is no longer afraid of mental health wellness. The change is not about abandoning faith. It’s about transforming and aligning faith with truth.

Therapy, combined with prayer, brings things to the surface. Through the guidance of wise counselors, pastors, and mental health professionals, Gen X individuals come to understand God’s extension of grace.

Counseling is a biblical tool that God can use to bring restoration. Faith and therapy can work together to promote healing that affects both the mind and the soul. Through listening, empathy, and understanding, Christian counselors provide a pathway for Gen X Christians to experience a spiritual awakening that overcomes the stigma of being a latchkey kid. Gen X is learning that vulnerability does not weaken faith, and the courage to seek help is not a rejection of prayer.

The Role of the Church Today

Today’s church has an opportunity to redeem what was once neglected. Many Gen X believers are serving in leadership, raising children, mentoring the younger generation, or guiding ministries. They are becoming more emotionally honest in the church. Those who feel unseen can find a refuge in churches that address mental health with compassion and biblical truth.

Pastors and ministry leaders who encourage counseling and openness help dismantle the old taboo that faith and therapy are mutually exclusive. Encouragement and support are spiritual disciplines that create space for confession, lament, and healing. The churches that promote this reflect the heart of Christ, who forgives and restores.

Hope and Restoration for a Healing Generation

Gen X may have learned how to be silent in their childhood, but many are now discovering a new language of grace. They are learning to rest, admit their weaknesses, and believe that God’s strength is made perfect in their imperfections.

Even though they face fatigue or reflection in their midlife, some are beginning to see it as a season of renewal. They now understand that the God who saw their quiet endurance as children is now inviting them to experience His rest as adults.

And after you have suffered a little while, the God of all grace, who has called you to his eternal glory in Christ, will himself restore, confirm, strengthen, and establish you. – 1 Peter 5:10, ESV

Wellness Is Possible

Standing at a crossroads, carrying the memory of what was and the promise of transformation, Gen X individuals are now able to grasp the openness of healing in the form of faith-based Christian counseling. They are learning how to dismantle the walls that helped them survive so they can be restored.

Connecting with a Christian counselor can lead to a transformed life that is not based on hiding emotions. By learning to implement skills that break the walls of silence and heal childhood wounds, Gen X individuals can experience mental health wellness that encourages them to find strength amid restoration.

For more information about overcoming the taboo mindset about mental health wellness, contact your local Christian counseling service. Begin your journey to breaking free from the silence of living strong as a Gen X individual.

item.title: True Transformation: Rewiring the Brain with Healthy Thoughts
item.description:
Have you ever thought, “I want transformation but don’t know how to achieve it”? Or “Why am I not experiencing lasting change?” Have you tried hard to make some changes in your life, but you still feel little to no progress? Or maybe you experienced some good changes, but they did not last long? What is the key to authentic and lasting transformation? The answer is in our thoughts.

The Garden Image

Let me explain with an image. Imagine your mental health is a large garden. The goal is to keep the garden flourishing with good plant life, which will represent mental health wellness. Now imagine the problem you are facing is a standard garden weed. The weed is toxic to your garden and must be removed. The weed can be anxiety, anger outbursts, depression, addiction, trauma, relationship discord, etc.

Removing the weed will keep away significant damage to your mental health. Some people will attempt to fix the problem by removing the stems and leaves and anything else they can see above the soil. They walk away thinking, “The weed is gone, so the problem is solved.” But they return in a few months to find that the same garden weed returned with more leaves and stems. How could it possibly have grown back?

As you can guess, the roots of the weed remained in the soil, which only made the problem appear to be gone. The person failed to pull the garden weed out by the roots. As long as the roots remain, the problem remains, which means no real lasting change can take place.

Now let me give some explanation of what the different parts of the weed represent. The stems and leaves of the garden weed represent behaviors and feelings. The roots of the garden weed represent our thoughts.

Understandably, we focus on the behaviors quite a bit to fix the problem because it is what we are seeing. Behaviors are everything from substance use and running away to playing and laughing. We can try to change our behaviors and feelings all day long but still have no real lasting change. Psychology teaches us that our thoughts affect our emotions and then our emotions affect our behaviors, and then our behaviors create our experiences.

So, for authentic and lasting change to take place, we need to examine the thoughts because they are the root, the epicenter, of everything that is happening. We must examine the deepest part of ourselves because this holds the greatest power to affect our entire psyche. This means that (in this image) the root of the weed needs to be fully removed in order for there to be change.

But it does not stop there. Not only does the root of the weed need to be removed, but it also needs to be replaced with a far healthier plant (a healthier thought). When we have healthy thoughts, incredible, lasting transformation starts to take place.

Rewiring the Brain

So now that we understand that the root of the garden weed is toxic thoughts (untruthful, unhelpful, distorted thinking), what do we do about it? The answer is in rewiring the brain.

God created our brains in a way to have the ability to remap and rewire themselves. Romans 12:2 states, “Do not conform to the pattern of this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind.” In today’s world, we know this concept formally as neuroplasticity and cognitive restructuring.

Neuroplasticity is the remarkable ability of the nervous system to change, adapt, and reorganize its physical structure and functional connections throughout your life. It is the biological mechanism that allows the brain to learn new skills, recover from injuries, and adapt to changing environments.

This means that the transformation we seek doesn’t begin with changing circumstances or relationships. Transformation starts in our minds. We must shift the way we think in order to get the transformation we want. So, let’s begin by understanding some basic neuroscience.

Every time you have a thought, a neural pathway is created or reused in your brain. The more you have a particular thought, the stronger that neural pathway becomes and eventually becomes an automatic thought. Automatic thoughts are pathways in our mind that we have used so many times that they are instantly the way we think about a certain situation, person, or stimulus.

The first thing to do is to record these thoughts, formally known as a Thought Record. In the world of cognitive behavioral therapy, we call this cognitive restructuring. We select one thought at a time and put it on trial to challenge its validity. We ask, “Is this true? Is this hurting me or helping me? Is this thought based on objective facts?” When we find that a thought is untruthful, distorted, and only hurting us, we can then identify that as a toxic thought.

Once we have identified a toxic thought, we then select a replacement thought that is truthful, healthy, and helpful. God, being the divine architect of our brains, knows that the way to fix toxic thinking is by deliberately focusing our thoughts on what is healthy and helpful. Philippians 4:13 instructs us to focus our thoughts on what is true, noble, right, pure, lovely, admirable, excellent, and praiseworthy.

And again, science is just now catching up to this. Neuroscience proves Philippians 4:13 by showing us how new neural pathways form when we have a thought. Studies and research conclude that healthy, helpful thoughts bring life and wellness to our bodies.

The antidote to toxic thinking is to intentionally focus on and rehash thoughts that are true, noble, right, pure, lovely, admirable, excellent, and praiseworthy. This is the game changer. So, the only way to make that toxic thought stop is to replace it with a new thought.

Now the next part takes discipline and practice. We live in a culture of fast-paced results, but our brain does not operate in the same way. Our brain needs significant repetition to wire in an automatic thought. The studies and research on neuroplasticity have found that the new thought needs to be rehearsed enough to get wired into the brain.

In one study, participants were directed to rehearse their new healthy thought by taking five minutes every day to repeat the healthy thought out loud or write it down over and over again. The results showed that many participants had successfully rewired their brain with the new healthy thought by day sixty-three. The toxic thought naturally eased in intensity, and for many, the toxic thought ceased.

The new wiring of healthy thought results in more positive emotions (peace, optimism, contentment) and then creates more desired behaviors (restful sleep, connecting with others, responding calmly to stress). This is what we want in our mental health garden. Pulling out weeds and then planting healthy plants is the key to lasting change.

Remember, your life will not change until your mind changes. You are only limited by how you see yourself and how you choose to think. Your mind and thoughts are the game changer to true and lasting transformation.

How To Rewire Your Mind

Write down all your thoughts (a Thought Record)

Put your thoughts on trial Determine whether it is healthy, helpful, and truthful, or untruthful, hurtful, and toxic.

To help determine if the thought is healthy or toxic, ask the following: Is this based on facts? What are the objective facts here? Did I confirm that my interpretation is based on reality? Did the person actually say that to me? Is there another way I could look at this? Did that actually happen? Does this thought make me feel worse, or does it make things feel more manageable?

Select a new healthy thought

Working on this with a therapist or good friend is always helpful because they can offer a new way of thinking about this thought that you likely have not considered before.

Meditate on this new thought through active repetition every day Reserve five minutes every day to rehearse the new healthy thought by saying it out loud or writing it. Continue this routine until the new thought becomes an automatic thought. Anticipate about two months to notice real change and a transformation that lasts a lifetime.

Repeat this process with every toxic thought This is a lifelong skill to commit to.

Example

The automatic thought: “I can’t do anything right.”

Challenge the thought with questions: What exactly do I feel I have not done right? Is it really true that everything I have done is wrong? Is this thought hurting me or is it helping me?

Consider the answers: This thought makes me feel bad, which means it is hurting me. No, it is not true that everything I have done is wrong. I have indeed done a few things wrong because my coworker verbally told me that I did not complete certain tasks needed before closing the shop. But there are a lot of things I have done correctly at work. I know this because my supervisor thanked me for the good work.

Select a new healthy thought: “Sometimes I make mistakes. I am human, I am not perfect, and mistakes are part of life. There are a lot of things I do correctly. I can choose to learn from my mistakes.”

item.title: Anger Management Strategies to Help You Control Your Anger
item.description:
Anger is a powerful emotion that can derail your life if you allow it. Not only can unbridled anger cloud your judgment, but it can also rob you of your sense of peace while damaging relationships, sometimes irreparably. As troublesome as it is, we should remember that anger isn’t necessarily sinful or against God’s will for our lives. Scripture reminds us, “Be angry and do not sin; do not let the sun go down on your anger.” (Ephesians 4:26, ESV)

While anger isn’t necessarily sinful, the challenge that we all face is that anger can be difficult to manage. It’s way too easy for justifiable or righteous anger to quickly morph into the sort of anger that dishonors the Lord and others. What starts well and good can become damaging to your relational, emotional, and mental well-being. Having good anger management strategies can help you maintain a healthy balance.

Unpacking the Impact of Anger

When you feel anger rising inside of you, usually it’s because it’s been triggered by something. You may have been snubbed at work by a colleague, or your loved one left you feeling unheard. Perhaps someone took advantage of you, or you witnessed something manifestly unjust. Whatever it is, one of the emotional responses to such situations is anger, and that anger is often appropriate.

Anger can be overwhelming, and indulging it may seem so rewarding in the moment. Letting choice words fly at someone who cut you off in traffic can give you a sense of accomplishment or victory. I sure told them, we might say to ourselves. It is way too easy to go over the line and say too much, say something you regret, or act recklessly without regard to how those words or actions feel to other people.

It may be helpful to picture anger like a wild bronco that may have placid moments, but that can change in an instant. It’s not wise to turn your back or let your guard down around them. Uncontrolled anger can wreak havoc in your life by stirring up conflict, leading you to utter hurtful words you otherwise wouldn’t, or taking you down the path to actions you later regret.

There is a Proverb that says, “An angry person stirs up conflict, and a hot-tempered person commits many sins.” (Proverbs 29:22, NIV) If anger begins controlling you, it becomes a chronic problem. Such anger has spiritual consequences, such as derailing your walk with the Lord (James 1:19-22). Chronic anger can also increase your stress levels and negatively impact your physical health by increasing your blood pressure and the risk of heart disease.

Besides these effects of uncontrolled anger, there can be a relational cost to anger, too. Anger can create deep wounds between loved ones, and those wounds can be slow to heal. Anger can also build walls between people, especially when that anger makes them feel unsafe around you. Anger, then, can be quite devastating.

The Blessings of Better Anger Management

The above probably gives anger a bad rap by pointing out all of the negative impacts of anger. Remember, anger isn’t sinful in itself. There is something to be said for dealing with anger in a healthy and constructive way. Anger can be a tool used for growth and renewal, and it’s not just destructive.

An example of this is when you feel unheard by a loved one. The feelings of anger can be handled well or poorly. The unhealthy route would include giving them the silent treatment in response or shouting at them to make yourself heard. The healthy option would include listening to that anger and discerning what lies at the root of it, and then pursuing dialogue with your loved one.

It is possible to express anger in healthy ways that build stronger relationships. Anger can function like a check engine light to let you know what’s happening inside you. Responding appropriately to those cues helps you communicate your needs effectively with others. This can mean fostering deeper trust and intimacy when you give gentle responses to tense situations.

Being in control of your anger and managing it well can also mean better health as you lower your stress levels, open yourself up more to the Lord’s peace, and yield more and more to the Spirit’s guidance. You’re better able to live well with yourself and with others when you can manage your emotions effectively.

Why Some Anger Management Strategies Fail

There are many benefits to managing your anger well. However, there are pitfalls along that path, and being aware of them can help you to be fruitful as you try to keep your anger in check.

Anger management strategies can fail or fall short when they are only skin deep. There is a strategy where you count slowly down from ten, and it’s a way to help you slow down before you respond rashly. This strategy does work in the moment, but it’s important to address the underlying heart issues. Anger can resurface and become harder to control.

Sticking with anger management strategies can also be difficult if you’re relying solely on willpower. For sustained and lasting change, we need the Lord’s help as well as accountability from others. The encouragement and support we get from other people can help us stay on the path, and the work of the Spirit in us can bring about true transformation in our hearts.

In other circumstances, anger management strategies don’t stick because we ignore the root causes of anger. Anger may be a momentary response, but many other things, such as learned patterns of behavior, often inform it. Other underlying causes of anger could be stress, unforgiveness, or unresolved trauma, which can fuel your anger and unhealthy responses to situations.

Awareness of these potential pitfalls can help you make good use of anger management strategies that help you keep anger in check. At the same time, you can address the deeper issues that could be informing your anger.

Effective Anger Management Strategies to Help You Control Anger

There are many strategies that you can use to help you manage your anger. It’s important to remember that anger management isn’t about suppressing your anger or pretending it doesn’t exist. Those are different ways of handling anger poorly. Rather, the goal is to develop a healthy relationship with your anger, to be able to understand your own anger, and channel it constructively instead of letting it take the reins.

Some effective anger management strategies include the following:

Pause, and pray: Allow yourself to count down from ten, or to leave the room briefly when you can, to allow yourself space to calm down. Stepping out of the situation can make a difference. When you feel anger rising, pause, breathe, and pray. Ask the Lord to help you stay calm and respond wisely, instead of being guided by your emotions.

Identify your triggers: Your anger works in ways that are unique to you. Reflect on the situations that tend to make your anger flare up. Recognize your own patterns of anger, like when you’re tired, hungry, stressed, or feeling vulnerable. Knowing these patterns helps you to anticipate your anger and manage it before it flares up or escalates.

Reframe your thoughts: Often, anger can be magnified because of our thinking patterns. If someone makes a hurtful joke or comment, it might not necessarily be intentional. Assuming it is can cause anger to flare up. It’s better to presume otherwise until you have further information. Meditating on Scripture about patience and self-control can also help to reshape your responses to triggering situations.

Use healthy outlets: Anger ought to be expressed, and there are healthy ways to do this. Using art or other forms of creative expression like writing, exercise and other physical activity, or talking things out with a trusted confidante can help you to release the tension of anger without damaging yourself or other people.

Practice forgiveness: Grudges and resentment can harbor and nurture anger. Instead, choose to forgive, releasing yourself from the burden of resentment or the need to get even.

Develop communication and problem-solving skills: There are times when you feel angry because you feel helpless or can’t express your concerns clearly. When you can plan and act to overcome challenges, and when you can work through issues amicably, it can prevent frustrations from taking over.

Seek help: Anger management therapy can help you dig deep to understand the underlying causes of your anger. You can also learn how to reframe your thoughts and implement strategies to help keep your anger under control. Help isn’t far from you; reach out to our office to connect with an anger management counselor today.

item.title: Breaking Out of the Sleep Anxiety Spiral
item.description:
Some people get to a certain age, and they realize that they have been exhausted for months or even years. Sleep loss affects an array of people, from teens in the middle of exams, new parents adjusting to the demands of an infant, or elderly people dealing with rapid changes in their lives. Some people are simply tired because events like these are demanding, but many people are tired because they have sleep anxiety.

Sleep anxiety is not the same as insomnia; it is the things that cause insomnia. It is the fear you start to feel as bedtime nears, as you worry that you will not fall asleep. It is the dread you feel when you wake up in the middle of the night and see that it is only midnight. You spend hours in bed, willing yourself to sleep, but failing. You can’t help but think about your day tomorrow and the consequences of losing sleep.

Sleep anxiety is debilitating, but it can be fixed without medication or substances. Studies have shown that medication does not help with sleep anxiety in the long-term. When you begin to understand what is going on in your head and in your body, you will begin to unpack some of the anxiety surrounding your sleep problems, breaking the sleep anxiety spiral. Your overthinking might be the thing driving your sleep anxiety, but your mind is also the solution.

The Sleep Anxiety Spiral

The most frustrating thing about sleep anxiety is that it is self-perpetuating. You stress about not being able to fall asleep or stay asleep, and it is that stress that causes sleeplessness. It is like being so afraid of failing your driving test that you cannot concentrate and end up failing the test. It is a form of self-fulfilling prophecy.

Sleep anxiety doesn’t only cause you stress in the evenings, but it also affects your daytime routine. Many people believe that they can only function properly on eight solid hours of sleep per day. This is a common idea that intensifies sleep anxiety. It looks like this: you believe that you need eight hours of quality sleep per day, and so you become anxious that you won’t get that. Then it is your anxiety over not getting enough sleep that becomes the very thing preventing you from getting enough sleep.

There are things you can do and things you must keep from doing to break the sleep anxiety spiral. Overall, you must change your approach to sleep, change the way you think about sleep, and make some changes to your routine. By interrupting your thoughts and behavior this way, you are creating a new pattern for yourself, and it can adapt to your new lifestyle.

Things You Must Do to Interrupt Sleep Anxiety

There are several practical things that you can start doing to interrupt the sleep anxiety spiral. It is a good idea to speak with a doctor or specialist before starting this new regimen, or with anyone who can keep you accountable and provide support. These ideas range from simple tips to deeper and broader attitude changes.

Firstly, create a healthy bedtime routine and stick to it. Your body has a function called the circadian rhythm. This is a set of automatic responses that your central nervous system performs throughout the day to help you. When your brain registers that it is nearing bedtime, it will release a hormone called melatonin into your nervous system. This hormone brings down your cortisol levels, puts your bladder and bowels on pause for the night, and generally prepares your body to be inactive for the next eight to ten hours.

You can help your circadian rhythm in practical ways by following a 3-2-1 principle. Have your final meal of the night three hours before bedtime, have your final drink two hours before bedtime, and reduce screen time for the last hour before bed. This will prime your body for sleep even if your mind is overactive.

With sleep anxiety, you struggle to fall asleep, and you struggle to stay asleep. The first thing most people do when they wake up is to look at the clock and calculate how many hours of sleep they have left. Try taking away your ability to time-check. Remove clocks from your bedroom and place your phone far away from your bedside. This interrupts the compulsive time-checking and the anxiety that comes with it.

In a larger sense, you must change the way you think about sleeping. For example, you might believe that you can only function during the day if you have had more than six hours of sleep the night before.

The truth is that you can be perfectly functional on minimal sleep, even over a long period of time. New parents experience years of sleeplessness and still manage to get by successfully. Sometimes it is your internal beliefs about sleep that contribute the most to sleep anxiety.

Lean into the idea that you are going to be tired tomorrow, and that it’s okay. Accept whatever amount of sleep you get, whether it’s only a few solid hours. Think of nighttime as rest time rather than sleep time.

The fact that you are lying down in a relaxed, safe environment and not looking at screens is enough for your body; sleep would be a bonus. When you change the way you think about sleep, sleep anxiety begins to lose its footing and influence over your mind.

Things to Avoid While Dealing with Sleep Anxiety

It’s natural to feel helpless and overwhelmed with sleep anxiety, and many people resort to using medication and substances like alcohol to cope. These things might help get you some sleep occasionally, but there is a real danger of becoming dependent on them over time. If you have been using medication or substances to help with sleep anxiety, aim to stop using them entirely.

Avoiding screen time before bed and keeping clocks out of sight is good, but it’s also a good idea to get up if you wake up at a certain time. When you lie in bed chasing sleep, you tend to begin overthinking and stressing.

You could try using mindfulness techniques or tools like brain shuffling to get back to sleep, but it’s a better idea to get up and go to a quiet spot in the house for some reading or crafting. Try to avoid screens still, and it’s best not to eat or drink anything. Instead, doing a relaxed activity in a dimly lit room will help keep the anxiety at bay. Eventually, you will become sleepy again, at which point you can simply return to bed to sleep.

Many sleep-tracking apps try to address insomnia, but these have the opposite effect on sleep anxiety. When you have a visualization for how much sleep you’re not getting, that intensifies the anxiety you feel. The goal is to be rested, not to get the perfect amount of sleep each night. Avoid tracking your sleep or trying to meet sleep goals. Instead, aim to have a restful evening. If you fall asleep for a few hours, that’s great. If you don’t, it’s not the end of the world.

Sleep anxiety is difficult, but it’s a cycle you can break. It might not happen overnight, but if you can get to a place where you feel more rested and less anxious, you will have made incredible progress. Give yourself a break because you deserve it.

Some things are easier to face and overcome with someone on your side. Consider meeting with a counselor if your sleep anxiety has become overwhelming. If you don’t have a counselor, we hope that you can find someone suitable in our online catalog or by enlisting the help of our reception team.

item.title: Finding Freedom from Fear: A Christian Counselor’s Personal Story
item.description:
Fear is an essential survival mechanism that elicits both physical and emotional reactions. When you sense a threat, fear is protective. However, fear can be overwhelming if it is out of balance and out of proportion to the risks. Maintaining psychological balance requires an understanding of the nature of fear and practical coping strategies.

For God has not given us a spirit of fear, but of power and of love and of a sound mind – 2 Tim. 1:7, NKJV

My Journey Into Fear

Personally, I spent years living in fear. As a child, I was afraid of the dark. Fear followed me into adulthood, marriage, moving to a bigger city, then motherhood, and my home. Although I loved God and trusted Him, I couldn’t seem to silence the constant “what ifs” that stole my peace.

One thing that magnified my fears was the news. As long as I can remember, I’ve noticed a trend on the news and then eventually on social media: fear.

There is always something on the news or happening in the world that could make us fearful: wars, pandemics, health issues, job insecurity, the health and welfare of our children, other anxieties and phobias, etc. I got sucked into the news after 9/11. So, in 2020, after the news of the pandemic, I had to stop watching or reading the news.

I had faith; I believed in God, and deep down I knew He would protect us. But I couldn’t shake that grip that fear had on me. I would pray over our house, walk around and pray over our property, etc., but nothing seemed to help the fear subside.

I had trouble sleeping because of my fears of someone breaking into our home. I bought a little picture of an angel guarding a child’s bed and every night began to recite the passage that was printed on it: Psalm 4:8, “In peace I will lie down and sleep, for you alone, LORD, make me dwell in safety.”

I had been reading The Power of a Praying Parent by Stormie Omartian and read the chapter on fear, not just for my daughter, but for me. It was pretty humbling. I tried to read other books on fear, but they all dealt with things such as stage fright, asking for a raise, etc. Those are still real and debilitating fears, but I felt like I was the only person who was fearing for my life.

A Prisoner of Fear

Looking back, I realize I was truly a prisoner to my own mind and emotions. On top of the fear, I was dealing with so many other “issues.” God began to slowly peel away at those issues one by one, but it truly took faith to overcome the fear.

Neil T. Anderson (2017) reminds us, “Fear is a God-given natural response when our physical or psychological safety is threatened. Fear always has an object, that is something or someone, and that object must be both present and potent, that is perceived to have some power over us. It ceases to be a fear object when only one of those attributes is eliminated” (p. 28).

He goes on to explain, The fear of people, death, and Satan is the root of almost all fears. Death is still present since it is a real possibility, but once we believe in Jesus and accept Him as our Lord and Savior, it is no longer powerful (1 Cor. 15:54-55).

Although fear is a normal human reaction, sometimes anxiety and fear become more than occasional worry. I realize that, for some individuals, anxiety can involve biological, psychological, and environmental factors that require additional support. But for now, I am talking mostly about fear that is out of balance and has no real threat.

In counseling, we often talk about how our thoughts influence our emotions and behaviors. Fear thrives on repeated messages of danger, while faith grows when we intentionally focus on truth. Another perspective that helped me was understanding fear as misplaced faith – placing belief in what might go wrong rather than in God’s promises.

Looking back, I can see how fear grew stronger when I repeatedly focused on threatening information. The more I watched the news and imagined worst-case scenarios, the more my mind became trained to anticipate danger.

The Nature of Fear

As a counselor, I have seen how anxiety can affect even the strongest believers. Experiencing anxiety does not mean someone lacks faith, nor does seeking counseling, medical care, or medication indicate spiritual weakness.

God often works through the wisdom, support, and resources He provides through others. Just as we seek treatment for physical illnesses, there are times when receiving professional support for our mental and emotional well-being is an important part of healing.

One resource God used during my journey was a small booklet called Freedom From Fear. While I don’t believe one book is the answer for everyone, God used its biblical perspective to help me recognize how fear had shaped my thinking. For some reason, reading it made that little lightbulb in my brain turn on. I had that “Aha” moment.

“There are two spiritual laws at work in the world today: the law of the Spirit of life in Christ Jesus and the law of sin and death. The force of faith comes from life. The force of fear comes from death” (back cover). In the booklet, the law of reciprocals (“corresponding, but reversed or inverted” principles) is discussed in Romans 8:2: “For the law of the Spirit of life in Christ Jesus has made me free from the law of sin and death.”

Understanding that fear is just faith perverted (by Satan) opened my eyes. Satan is “limited to the forces of the world.” He cannot create or come up with new ideas. He just perverts the spiritual laws that are already in place. “Sin was not a new law. It was righteousness perverted. Death was life perverted. Hate was love perverted. Fear was faith perverted (pg. 5).”

In the Garden of Eden, after Adam and Eve sinned, the first words Adam spoke to God were, “I was afraid” (Genesis 3:10). The enemy is here to steal, kill, and destroy. So, he took the faith that Adam had, and it was turned to fear. I love where it’s explained, “The counterfeit never is as powerful as the real thing” (pg. 7). Therefore, we know that when we put faith to work, “it will always overcome fear.”

The Complexity of Anxiety and Fear

As I reflect on those years, I also recognize that fear and anxiety can be complex. While my journey involved learning to trust God more deeply and renew my mind with His Word, I realize that not everyone experiences fear in the same way.

Some people have lived through traumatic events, loss, abuse, or other painful experiences that leave their nervous system on high alert. Others struggle with anxiety disorders, panic attacks, obsessive thoughts, or other mental health concerns that involve biological, emotional, and environmental factors.

Practical Steps When Fear Feels Overwhelming

  • Identify the fearful thought.
  • Ask whether there is evidence of an actual present danger.
  • Compare that thought with God’s truth in Scripture.
  • Pray honestly about your fears.
  • Pray specific and related scriptures out loud (I will list some below).
  • Reach out to trusted believers or a counselor when fear becomes persistent or overwhelming.
  • Limit media that continually fuels fear.
  • Remember that courage often means moving forward while still feeling afraid.

For me, freedom came through prayer, Scripture, renewing my mind through books and other resources, and learning to trust God’s promises. For others, that journey may also include counseling, support groups, trauma work, medical care, or a combination of these resources. God can use all of these tools as part of His healing process.

But in our everyday Christian walk, we have to walk by faith. In doing so, we have to know the Word of God and stand on its principles. We have to know that Satan is under our feet because of what Jesus has done for us. As believers, we are free from every part of the curse.

So, why do we allow him to pull us around on strings of fear, worry, anxiety, depression, etc.? Yes, we are physical beings and will have physical problems, but God is bigger than any of our problems, and He has put other people – professionals – here on earth to help us walk through some of the pains of life.

Even though we know these truths, many of us still wrestle with fear, worry, anxiety, and discouragement. Sometimes these struggles are connected to painful experiences, ingrained thought patterns, or circumstances beyond our control. Yet God’s promises remain true. He meets us in our struggles and patiently helps us grow in faith as we learn to trust Him more fully.

For believers, Scripture is the foundation for confronting fear – both the fears rooted in reality and the ones shaped by our thoughts and emotions. God can also place different resources in our paths to help us confront fear and work through the layered process of renewing the mind. We can’t just stop at reading the Scripture; we have to believe it and apply it.

James 1:22 tells us, “But don’t just listen to God’s word. You must do what it says.” We have to speak the Word and believe what we are saying. When we speak His promises, we must remember the authority that we have through Jesus and speak it with confidence, not with hesitation.

As believers, we must take every thought captive (2 Cor. 10:5). Then, we must renew our minds with the Word of God (Rom. 12:2). I will share some of my favorite passages below. 365 references in the Bible say or address, “Do not fear.” Or as one of our friends says, “One ‘Do not fear’ for every day of the year!” (I love that!)

After I read Freedom from Fear, I knew that things were beginning to change in my thought life, but it wasn’t until a women’s retreat (my first retreat with my church) that I truly became free and broke off the chains of fear. I had gone to get away, enjoy myself, and, of course, for the great teaching I would receive, but I didn’t realize it would be life-changing.

I went away still battling fear, but returned home freed from the hurts, bitterness, worry, and the rest of the lies the enemy had been telling me at that time.

Fear once dictated many of my decisions, stole my peace, and kept me awake at night. Today, I still face circumstances that could make me fearful, but I no longer live under fear’s control. Freedom did not come overnight; it came through renewing my mind with God’s Word, learning to trust Him more deeply, and choosing faith one step at a time.

Anderson (2017) says, “Courage is not the absence of fear. Courage is choosing to live by faith and doing what is right in the face of perceived fear-objects. Behind every irrational fear is a lie, which must be identified. Ask the Lord to reveal to your mind the nature of your fears and the irrational lies that compel them” (2017, p. 28).

If fear has become a constant companion in your life, know that you are not alone. Whether through prayer, Scripture, counseling, supportive relationships, or a combination of these resources, healing is possible. The Lord is for you. And because He is for you, fear does not have to have the final word.

As I’ve shared, freedom from fear did not happen overnight for me. It was a process of learning to recognize fearful thoughts, replacing them with truth, and choosing – sometimes moment by moment – to trust God. Healing often works the same way. It may involve different resources that God provides. While the journey looks different for each person, we can take comfort in knowing that God walks with us through every step.

Bible Verses to Ponder

The LORD is my light and my salvation; whom shall I fear? The LORD is the strength of my life; of whom shall I be afraid? When evildoers came upon me to devour my flesh, my adversaries and my enemies, they stumbled and fell. Though a host encamp against me, my heart will not fear; Though war arises against me, in spite of this I shall be confident. – Psalm 27:1-3, NKJV

The LORD is for me; I will not fear; What can man do to me? – Psalm 118:6, NASB

Don’t be afraid of those who want to kill your body; they cannot touch your soul. Fear (reverence) only God, who can destroy both soul and body in hell. But the very hairs of your head are all numbered. so do not fear; you are more valuable than many sparrows. – Matthew 10:28, 30-31, NLT

Since the children have flesh and blood, he too shared in their humanity so that by his death he might break the power of him who holds the power of death – that is, the devil –  and free those who all their lives were held in slavery by their fear of death. – Hebrews 2:14-15, NIV

Seeking support is not a sign of weak faith. God often works through the wisdom, support, and resources He provides through others. Please give our reception team a call and schedule an appointment.

Anderson, N. T. (2017). The steps to freedom in Christ: A biblical guide to help you resolve personal and spiritual conflicts and become a fruitful disciple of Jesus. Bethany House Publishers
Kenneth Copeland. (1997). Freedom from fear. Kenneth Copeland Publications.

item.title: Overwhelming Anxiety in a Time of War: Finding Solid Ground Through Faith
item.description:
Here we are again. Breaking news, a new conflict has erupted in a distant land. We are glued to our televisions, computers, or smartphones, drawn in by a relentless news cycle that bring the unnerving feeling of uncertainty in a world that seems to be in constant turmoil.

As a chaplain in the Army Reserves and throughout my 21-year Army career, the all too familiar phone calls from friends and loved ones panicking over a news story of new conflict have been a frequent reminder that overwhelming anxiety during times of war impact those I love the most more than me.

We live in an age when technology keeps us connected to conflicts, even though they happen far away. We find the weight of what’s unfolding in the world, settling into our homes as if it is there to take charge. This can bring about anxiety, especially during war.

Wartime stress isn’t confined to the battlefield or the families waiting by the phone. It will creep into ordinary life, the grocery store, the drive to work, and even in the moments before sleep. Overwhelming anxiety in the middle of a global conflict is real, valid, and something that far more people of faith grapple with than most of us are willing to admit.

Wartime stress can feel invisible from the inside, even as everything on the outside looks completely normal. We go to work. We show up for our family and sit in the pews on Sunday morning. In fact, as pastor of a local church, there have been times when I have to walk in on a Sunday morning with more questions than answers about conflicts erupting around the world.

At times I wonder, Will it be me called up to go next while at the same time trying to reassure my family, friends, and congregants? The reality is that underneath all the functioning is something that feels increasingly fragile. If you feel like this, you’re not alone, and you’re not without hope.

The Lord is my shepherd; I shall not want. He makes me lie down in green pastures. He leads me beside still waters. He restores my soul. – Psalm 23:1–3, ESV

What Wartime Stress Actually Does to You

Our nervous system was not designed to absorb a continuous stream of crises. Still, with today’s technology, that is what happens: conflict dominates the news cycle and social media feeds. It leads to the sense that the world is unstable. Even though we’re not in a war zone, our bodies respond to this threat in measurable ways.

Our sleep becomes unreliable, and our concentration slips. We find that we’re easily startled and emotionally short-tempered with the people we love at the end of the day. We are exhausted beyond the point where rest can fix it. We find ourselves constantly hooked on scrolling through the feeds for updates and news.

We think that being constantly informed is a way of restoring a sense of control, even when we have no direct connection to the conflict. Compassion fatigue and secondary trauma are real. The grief we experience when we watch human suffering from a distance lands somewhere in the body and the mind, and does not dissolve simply because you step away from the computer or set down the phone.

For Christians, there’s an additional weight that comes in the quiet voice whispering that feeling afraid means you’re not trusting God. This internal pressure adds to the weight of the stress that we already carry simply because we care. Even in this, we can rest in God’s protection:

For he will hide me in his shelter in the day of trouble; he will conceal me under the cover of his tent; he will lift me high upon a rock. – Psalm 27:5, ESV

When Overwhelming Anxiety Becomes a Daily Reality

There is a difference between feeling concerned about what is happening and feeling consumed by it. Overwhelming anxiety goes past awareness and into something that disrupts our ability to engage in our daily lives. We wake up dreading the day before it has even begun. When joy feels completely inaccessible, we find ourselves mentally rehearsing a worst-case scenario in a loop that runs on its own, whether you want it to or not.

Military families, people connected to the conflict, or those who carry unresolved trauma from their own history find that wartime news triggers responses that reach well beyond ordinary worry. The result is that our minds draw connections between what is happening in the present and old wounds that were never fully healed. Suddenly, what we see unfolding across the world feels personal.

The Place Where Faith and Mental Health Meet

Some faith communities believe anxiety is a spiritual problem. The mindset in some of these communities is that praying more, studying the Bible more, and trusting God more will remove the fear that wartime news has created. Spiritual disciplines are valuable, and Scripture speaks to anxiety. The writers of the Psalms were not strangers to wartime, grief, or despair. It was all brought before God, honestly and openly, and without the performance of having it all together.

Anxiety is not eliminated by faith, but the foundation of faith does not shift when everything around you does. Faith offers a perspective that goes beyond the present moment into something eternal. It connects us to a body of believers who are meant to carry each other through the hard seasons. Christian counselors work in a way that integrates the realities of spiritual and psychological thought processes and understand that both matter.

With support, you can learn to handle your anxiety. The key is knowing what to do with it.

Do not be anxious about anything, but in everything by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let your requests be made known to God. And the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, will guard your hearts and your minds in Christ Jesus. – Philippians 4:6–7, ESV

Finding Your Footing: Practical Steps Toward Overwhelming Anxiety Relief

Navigating overwhelming anxiety is not a one-size-fits-all process. Several practices can help us navigate a world where news is accessible every hour of the day. The first step is to limit our consumption to a defined window during the day and allow our nervous system to settle.

Making time for physical movement helps the body process stress hormones instead of accumulating them. Practices that ground us and redirect our attention to what is present and immediate interrupt the mental loops that keep anxiety running.

During a season of sustained stress and isolation, connection matters. Having honest conversations with a trusted friend or a small group that is not afraid of hard questions can build a defense against the feeling of impending doom.

Christian counselors understand the intersection of faith and mental health. They can encourage you to name what you’ve been quietly carrying. This is the first real step toward something better. Reaching out for help can be difficult, but it is a courageous step toward releasing wartime anxiety.

Hope When You Battle Anxiety

The world has had its share of war, and each generation has faced the challenge of living faithfully amid it. This doesn’t make it easier, and it doesn’t reduce the anxiety or lessen the weight of concern. But it does mean that each of us is not the first person to bring fear and faith into the same room and ask God how to handle them both.

We’re not spiritually deficient or failing. We are human, and we are living through a season that is asking a great deal of each of us.

The great thing is, we don’t have to figure it out alone. There is grace in asking for help from God, who holds all things, and from Christian counselors who are trained, compassionate, and ready to walk alongside us. The possibility of healing from wartime stress and anxiety is in process, and it is in reach no matter when we decide to begin.

If you are experiencing overwhelming anxiety related to wartime stress, or you have a loved one who is grappling with it, there are people to help. Daily life doesn’t have to feel difficult, regardless of what’s happening in the world. You can contact our reception team to schedule a time to meet with a counselor who can help you navigate this season of anxiety.
