item.title: Understanding the Types of BPD and Their Connection to Substance Abuse
item.description:
Borderline personality disorder (BPD) affects how individuals experience themselves and relate to the world around them. Seeking relief from the emotional intensity that comes with BPD, individuals sometimes turn to substance abuse as a common coping mechanism. To understand why some people find themselves caught in patterns that they want to escape, we first have to understand the types of BPD and how they intersect with addiction.

There is a relationship between these two struggles that goes beyond a simple cause-and-effect. It reflects deeper questions about identity, managing pain, and a human need for stability. The way BPD manifests can determine not only how someone experiences their internal world, but which substances they turn to, and why. These distinctions are essential to break free from the cycle of emotional dysregulation and addiction.

Four Patterns Common Across the Multiple Types of BPD

Because each person is unique, borderline personality disorder doesn’t present the same way in everyone. Four primary patterns help explain the different ways that BPD manifests. These types of BPD are not meant to box people into categories concretely, but rather, they help us understand the ways emotional dysregulation shows up in real life. By recognizing which patterns resonate most with an individual, Christian counselors can guide treatment and offer hope that recovery is possible.

The discouraged type: This form of BPD often appears in people who seem dependent and seek constant reassurance while struggling with feelings of worthlessness. These individuals may appear passive or submissive in relationships and avoid confrontation, even when it would be healthy.

The impulsive type: Those who manifest this type of BPD often engage in risk-taking behaviors and emotional outbursts without concern for consequences. People who struggle with this form of BPD typically act on every feeling without pausing to consider the outcome, and they chase experiences that provide immediate gratification or distraction from inner emptiness.

The petulant type: This form of BPD involves stubborn negativity and feeling misunderstood, which results in pushing others away by simultaneously fearing abandonment. Individuals struggling with this pattern often feel like victims of their circumstances and may express bitterness or resentment toward those trying to help.

The self-destructive type: This pattern of BPD manifests in harmful behaviors directed inward, which include substance abuse, self-harm, or extreme risk-taking to manage unbearable emotional pain. Individuals of this type are the most visibly concerning. They seem intent on destroying themselves, even though self-harm isn’t about wanting to die. It’s about making internal pain visible.

Each of these patterns reflects a different strategy for managing the emotional dysregulation that is at the heart of BPD. Many individuals display characteristics from multiple types, and patterns can shift over time, so these categories are not considered rigid.

The consistency across these patterns is the intense fear of abandonment, unstable self-image, and difficulty regulating emotions that define the disorder. Adding substance abuse to this already intense struggle starts as an attempt to navigate the emotional turbulence that feels impossible to manage any other way.

Why Substance Abuse Co-Occurs with BPD

The connection between BPD and addiction is not coincidental. Most individuals diagnosed with BPD also struggle with substance use disorders. Because BPD creates an emotionally intense environment, substances often offer temporary relief from these struggles.

An individual experiencing rapid mood swings, chronic feelings of emptiness, and a fear of abandonment turns to alcohol or other substances to quiet the internal chaos. Substances only provide a brief escape from emotions that feel overwhelming and unmanageable.

Self-medication is not the only challenge with substance abuse and BPD. The brain chemistry is changed due to substance use, which can worsen BPD symptoms and create a cycle where each issue amplifies the other. Impulsivity is a core feature of BPD, and it can become more pronounced under the influence of substances, and emotional regulation becomes nearly impossible.

Christian counselors recognize that both conditions require integrated treatment. They emphasize that addressing one only leaves the underlying vulnerabilities untouched. The path to healing requires understanding how these struggles reinforce each other and learning how to cultivate healthier ways to cope with emotional pain. One good place to start is with encouraging Scriptures:

Cast your burden upon the Lord and He will sustain you; He will never allow the righteous to be shaken. – Psalm 55:22, NASB

How Different Types of BPD Influence Substance Use Patterns

A specific pattern of BPD often shapes the relationship an individual has with substances. Impulsive-type individuals engage in binge drinking or experiment with multiple substances, trying to find a thrill and temporary relief from boredom or inner emptiness.

Individuals who struggle with the self-destructive type of BPD may use substances deliberately to harm themselves or engage in dangerous combinations of risky behaviors. They are less concerned with pleasure and more focused on punishing themselves or numbing severe emotional pain.

Individuals who struggle with the discouraged type often use substances to cope with feelings of hopelessness and inadequacy. Using substances becomes an internal coping mechanism to numb the discouraging feelings.

The individual who suffers from the petulant type of BPD faces a more complex dynamic when it comes to substance use. They may engage in substance use in response to a perceived rejection or conflict. The result is a pattern where relationship struggles trigger substance use, which creates more relationship problems.

Christian counselors understand these patterns and can develop treatment approaches that address the specific needs of each individual who struggles with substance use and BPD. The goal is to build healthier ways to manage emotional experiences that made substances feel necessary in the first place.

Still, we are all reminded of Jesus’ words:

“Come to Me, all who are weary and burdened, and I will give you rest.” – Matthew 11:28, NASB

The Path Toward Integrated Healing

Co-occurring BPD and substance abuse recovery requires addressing both conditions simultaneously. If BPD remains untreated, traditional addiction treatment fails because the emotional dysregulation continues to drive the compulsion toward substances.

On the other hand, if BPD is treated without addressing active addiction, the treatment is ineffective because substances interfere with the ability to develop healthy coping strategies. Through integrated treatment, individuals learn to recognize that these conditions exist in relationship to one another and must be addressed together.

Dialectical behavior therapy (DBT) has become an effective treatment plan for individuals dealing with both BPD and substance abuse. Through this approach, individuals learn specific skills to manage distress, tolerate stress, and build more effective relationships.

Christian counselors often integrate faith-based perspectives and evidence-based treatments to help clients understand their value in Christ as they develop practical tools to manage symptoms. This process involves learning that emotions do not have to be escaped or numbed. Even intense emotions can be experienced, understood, and regulated in healthy ways.

Finding the Support You Need

The relationship between BPD and substance abuse is a reflection of a human tendency to seek relief from pain through whatever feels available. For treatment to be effective, individuals must understand the different patterns of BPD and how they intersect with addiction.

Each type of BPD – the discouraged, the impulsive, the petulant, or the self-destructive – presents a unique challenge and strength in the recovery process. The consistency is the need for integrated treatment that addresses both the emotional dysregulation involved with BPD and addictive patterns.

Healthy recovery includes building new skills, developing healthier coping mechanisms, and discovering that lasting peace isn’t found by escaping emotions. Instead, you can learn to navigate feelings with grace, support, and God’s Word.

If you or someone you know is facing the complex challenges of BPD and substance abuse, professional support can make a meaningful difference in your recovery. Christian counselors are trained to integrate faith-based encouragement with evidence-based treatment to help you navigate this journey and find lasting recovery.

Reach out to our office and connect with a Christian counselor who can help you take the first step toward integrated care for these struggles.

item.title: What Moral Scrupulosity Feels Like
item.description:
It’s admirable when people strive to be decent and morally upstanding, especially when they are setting an example to others. However, sometimes there is something sinister and overwhelming that drives certain people to be good. Moral scrupulosity is a type of Obsessive Compulsive Disorder (OCD) that urges a person to become intensely preoccupied with being a good person.

Sadly, it also causes a person to feel extreme anxiety, guilt, shame, exhaustion, and fear of being exposed as a fraud. It is as if they have a voice in their head constantly criticizing their actions, shining a spotlight on their mistakes, and making their small errors feel like unforgivable sins.

Being a decent person takes effort, and it’s not always easy to make the right choices. However, moral OCD causes intense distortions in a person’s view of themselves. Even a person who has a solid reputation can end up feeling like a moral failure because of the intrusive thoughts that surround moral OCD.

As with all forms of Obsessive Compulsive Disorder, it is possible to treat moral scrupulosity. First, however, you must understand how and to what extent it is affecting you.

Not Just About People-Pleasing

On the surface of things, moral scrupulosity often looks a lot like people-pleasing. People-pleasers need more than the average amount of reassurance from others, and the same is true for those with moral OCD. Both people-pleasers and those with moral scrupulosity try to keep others happy, and both want to be seen as kind, thoughtful, generous, and decent. The difference lies in their inner monologue and motivations.

People-pleasers feel the need to make others happy and to keep the peace in every environment. They will compromise their boundaries, disregard their personal preferences, and allow themselves to be taken advantage of to a degree. However, people pleasers do not experience the same inner monologue and intrusive thoughts as those with OCD. Also, people-pleasing habits greatly differ from OCD compulsions.

Moral scrupulosity hijacks a person’s conscience and takes over their actions. As with other kinds of OCD, there is a voice in their head constantly criticizing and challenging them to do certain things, or ridiculing them for not doing certain things.

For example, something as simple as drinking from a plastic straw can spark internal turmoil for someone with moral OCD. A people-pleaser might feel a twinge of guilt for the environment while sipping from a plastic straw. A person with moral scrupulosity will inwardly berate themselves for hours, framing this simple act as hypocrisy and moral failure.

What Moral Scrupulosity Sounds Like

There are two components to every type of obsessive compulsive disorder: intrusive thoughts and ritualistic or habitual actions. Moral scrupulosity is a ridiculing, criticizing, and sometimes threatening inner voice that spurs panic, fear, anxiety, and shame. It might be an echo of someone you know, or it might take on the quality of your own voice, but more cruel.

You will have thoughts like, “Who do you think you are, pretending to be like this?” or “You are being fake, and everyone will notice.” Sometimes your efforts will be singled out, and you will have thoughts like, “No matter what you do, you will never reach the standards you should,” or “You should have felt worse about that.”

None of these thoughts comes anything close to being positive, encouraging, or uplifting, and only results in you feeling worse about yourself. Most of them will have you questioning your self-worth, and some will cause you to wonder if you are a sociopath, a narcissist, or something worse.

Moral Scrupulosity in Action

Moral OCD mostly exists in your head. As with all OCD, the intrusive thoughts frequently lead to compulsive behavior and ritualistic habits. Many of these habits don’t appear to be obsessive or compulsive, but they are connected to the feelings that come from moral scrupulosity.

Some of the most common habits connected to moral scrupulosity are confessing, apologizing, and seeking reassurance. Feeling constantly guilty or on the verge of moral failure will lead you to scramble in an effort to save your reputation or prove your worth. You might have constant conversations with your spouse, partner, confidante, or pastor about your failures, or you might obsessively journal your fears and anxieties.

With moral OCD, you likely replay conversations over in your head, especially if you hurt someone with your words or were dishonest about something. Even when you feel as if you performed well socially, you still review your words and actions.

You will search for flaws, mistakes, or breaches of social etiquette, which you will use to berate yourself afterwards. These performance reviews become a ritual of sorts after any interaction or conversation you have.

Sometimes you will feel compelled to balance the scales with your actions. For example, in penitence for drinking from a plastic straw, you might donate more money than you can afford to a wildlife rescue fund. Actions like these, while hardly ever practical, become important ways for you to prove your morality and challenge your hypocrisy. They are also a way for you to punish personal wrongdoing and prove that you have leveled up your inner goodness.

Besides having a harsh inner-monitoring system, engaging in costly good deeds, and feeling compelled to confess your wrongdoing constantly, moral scrupulosity also leads to rigid rule-keeping. For you, rules are less about maintaining order or discipline and more about heavy ethics and social purity.

Guidelines become commandments, and failure on your behalf to comply with the code is an intense moral failing that you will struggle to repent from. You will likely also avoid getting involved in anything that feels morally gray or ambiguous. This leads you to pass up certain job opportunities, relationships, or hobbies if they seem like they will lead down a morally dubious path.

Free To Fail

As with all forms of OCD, moral scrupulosity is treatable with certain therapies. Forefront among these is Cognitive Behavioral Therapy and Exposure and Response Prevention (ERP). Recognizing the impact of your thoughts and actions is the start, and from there, you must be willing to feel uncomfortable as your worldview and belief system are challenged.

Recovery from moral OCD can only be gradual. You cannot change intrusive thoughts and compulsive actions overnight, nor would it be healthy if you could. CBT challenges the inner beliefs that surround moral scrupulosity, and ERP exposes you to different thoughts and challenges you to try new actions in response to them.

At first, it is unnerving to replace automatic thoughts like “I am a terrible person” with new thoughts like “Even when I make a mistake, I remain a decent person.” In time, your reflexive thoughts and actions begin to shift, and you will find yourself less preoccupied with your own failures and more focused on your triumphs and breakthroughs.

Somewhere out there, faith exists without fear, and love overrides guilt. Grace is not simply a concept applicable to other people who have earned it. Grace is a force that changes those who are most in need of it and most undeserving of it. Although it might be hard to believe, life does not have to be this difficult forever. Not only are you capable of change, but you are worthy of it.

Dealing with any type of OCD is overwhelming. Simply knowing you have an issue is only the start; now you must get help for it.

We host an online catalog that lists the details of many different counselors, where we hope you will find someone who can help you. If you would prefer to speak with people to arrange a meeting with a counselor, our reception team would love to help you. We hope you will find someone who can help you recover from OCD for good.

item.title: Chronic Loneliness and the Quiet Ache of Feeling Unseen
item.description:
Feeling invisible in a room full of people can leave you feeling disoriented. Whether it’s at a family gathering, a church service, or lunch with coworkers, something inside of you feels completely cut off from everyone around you. This isn’t a passing mood or a signal that you need a quiet evening at home. For most individuals, it’s a daily reality of chronic loneliness, even amid a busy schedule and a calendar full of social events.

There are no convenient moments for chronic loneliness to show up, but it is there, quiet and persistent, in places and circumstances that are supposed to feel the opposite of alone. This type of loneliness is difficult to address because it rarely looks like loneliness should. It’s not someone sitting alone with nowhere to go and no one to call.

Chronic loneliness is something different. It often affects people who are engaged, busy, and surrounded by family, church, and community. It is the hidden disconnection they feel underneath all of that activity. The first step in healing is to name it. Then, understanding follows, and healing can begin. Even Scripture encourages people to be honest about their loneliness:

Turn to me and be gracious to me, for I am lonely and afflicted. – Psalm 25:16, ESV

The Silence That Lives Inside a Crowded Room

It doesn’t seem right that it works this way; more people should mean more connections. Sitting in church pews with familiar faces or showing up to social events can still make people feel as though they are strangers in spaces where they should feel at home.

This issue goes far beyond not having people nearby. It includes something hard to name: a persistent sense that no one truly sees you, knows you, or notices if you come undone on the inside. This type of absence is more isolating than physical solitude could ever be.

We have societal expectations that shape this experience in ways we don’t always notice. A prevailing attitude that suggests that if you’re actively involved in a rooted community, especially a faith community, you should be fine. This generates an invisible pressure to perform kindness, even when the inside does not match the outside. People learn to smile, show up, and keep participating while feeling disconnected from the environments that foster belonging.

Christian counselors recognize this pattern before people are ready to acknowledge the loneliness outright. They show up exhausted, emotionally flat, and unsure, while nothing feels like it is working anymore. Proverbs 14 identifies this juxtaposition: “Even in laughter the heart may ache, and the end of joy may be grief.” (Proverbs 14:13, ESV)

What Chronic Loneliness Looks Like Beneath the Surface

Chronic loneliness is not a reflection of how many relationships you have. People can surround you, and you can still experience deep, persistent isolation. It is the distinction that matters, because it shifts the focus away from external circumstances toward the internal experience.

That experience is the quality of connection, the sense of genuinely being known, and the emotional safety that you feel in your relationships. When these elements are absent, a void registers in your body and mind, and it is difficult to ignore. It shows up as a quiet sense that something important is missing, and it is accompanied by emotional numbness.

There are social pressures that shape how you connect with others, and they contribute to this far more than you recognize. Competing values around being self-sufficient, productive, and having things together make it difficult to admit there’s something wrong.

Admitting loneliness is like admitting failure, especially in places of faith, where community has value and expectations. The result is a cycle that is difficult to break because of the avoidance of vulnerability. Pulling back deepens the disconnection that you’re trying to manage quietly, and the outcome is a persistent, unnamed suffering that rarely surfaces until something breaks open. Even in these lonely, broken places, you can hold onto the truth that God is near.

The Lord is near to the brokenhearted and saves the crushed in spirit. – Psalm 34:18, ESV

What Faith Says About Feeling This Type of Aloneness

God’s Word does not pretend that loneliness is not real. There are many honest prayers in the Bible that come from people who felt utterly isolated, such as prophets, kings in hiding, and disciples scattered by fear. The book of Psalms is filled with raw and unpolished cries that name emptiness and abandonment without any apology or qualification.

This is significant because it reminds us that profound loneliness is not a sign of insufficient faith or spiritual weakness. It is simply a human experience that God never asked anyone to minimize, deny, or quietly push through alone. God has always been acquainted with this kind of grief.

Faith does not offer an immediate answer to the ache, but it brings a genuine presence with it. God entered the human experience through Christ, and that His darkest hour was marked by complete abandonment. This doesn’t remove the pain of loneliness; instead, it gives it a witness. The experience of being unseen has already been brought before God, and He did not look away.

When you can bring your disconnection honestly before God and before a trusted community, something shifts. Christian counselors recognize that the intersection of spiritual and emotional health is central to their work. You cannot address the mind without addressing the spirit and expect it to be a lasting change.

Finding Your Way From Chronic Loneliness To Real Connection

Navigating chronic loneliness is not quick, and it is never linear. It requires that you learn to identify what a genuine connection actually feels like, not what it is supposed to look like from the outside. It is understanding what truly leaves you feeling less invisible and more fully yourself.

This process may include grieving the relationships and environments that were unable to offer that kind of safety. It is no secret that grief and loneliness are closely related. It will take patience and honest self-reflection to begin separating one from the other without losing sight of either.

When you reach out to a counselor, a trusted person in your community, or to God in prayer, that is the hardest and most important step. You can then move directly against the social pressure to handle things privately and maintain the appearance of self-sufficiency. This becomes the beginning of something real.

Christian counselors can help you examine the relational patterns that have kept you isolated and understand where those patterns developed. Then you can begin building toward the kind of connection that actually holds. Faith won’t ask you to be fine. It will ask you to be honest, and in that honesty is the very thing that interrupts the cycle.

Don’t Go Through This Alone

Chronic loneliness in the middle of a full life is a quiet form of pain that rarely announces itself and rarely receives the attention it deserves. This loneliness lives beneath conversations and behind smiles, hidden inside of people who have become quite practiced at looking fine while feeling far away from almost everyone around them. It is real, it matters, and it doesn’t have to remain a permanent aspect of your daily life.

There is nothing about your loneliness that disqualifies you from connection, community, or the nearness of God. He has never stopped moving toward the isolated and unseen. The journey toward connection begins with naming what is actually true. That means deciding to stop carrying what was never designed to be carried alone.

Whether you speak with a Christian counselor, reach out to someone you trust, sit in prayer, or acknowledge the weight of what you’ve been quietly holding, that is the beginning. And every beginning is always worth the step.

If loneliness has become a familiar or persistent part of your daily life, you do not have to face it alone. You can reach out to our office today and talk with our reception team to get started on your journey toward something better.

item.title: The Smile that Hides Repressed Anger
item.description:
Sometimes anger can convince people that it’s not there. It doesn’t always come with a loud voice in a heated moment. It can roll in quietly, disguised as a tight jaw, sudden irritability, or a withdrawn spirit. Repressed anger is a deceptive emotion that many people carry.

By the time it’s recognized, it’s been living under the surface for months, and it no longer feels like anger. It has been shaping decisions and relationships for months or even years in ways that are hard to trace back to the source. Scripture has clear guidelines on anger:

In your anger do not sin: Do not let the sun go down while you are still angry. – Ephesians 4:26, NIV

The Bible tells us that we will experience anger, but it’s what we do in that anger that creates the struggles and issues. Repressed anger is deeper than a spiritual choice. Managing anger by keeping it out of sight and holding it at a distance can be the underlying assumption in faith communities. But now we are coming to understand that this is not handling it well and that the hidden anger carries real weight.

What Repressed Anger Really Looks Like

Repressed anger doesn’t identify itself by a name. It tends to present as persistent, low-grade sadness or unexplained irritability. It could be a withdrawal from once meaningful relationships.

This surfaces when people have spent years managing emotional responses for the sake of others, leading them to lose touch with what they’re actually feeling beneath the surface. By the time the anger surfaces, it may have been buried so long that the person no longer recognizes it for what it is.

Each individual has a choice to establish internal honesty. It’s not comfortable, but it is necessary for understanding how we manage emotional responses. In places that feel complicated or unflattering, an individual can begin to know themselves fully. Faith communities tend to suggest that certain emotions make self-examination a spiritual risk.

When individuals or communities have framed anger as a sign of spiritual immaturity or something that a truly trusting person doesn’t experience, honesty becomes difficult to access. Just because an emotion isn’t acknowledged doesn’t mean it disappears. It just learns to live quietly until it can’t anymore.

Search me, God, and know my heart; test me and know my anxious thoughts. See if there is any offensive way in me, and lead me in the way everlasting. – Psalm 139:23-24, NIV

The Hidden Cost of Keeping the Peace

Sometimes peace is a cover for avoidance, wearing a spiritual name. This happens when it involves staying quiet even though something genuinely needs to be said or moving past a wound before it has been addressed honestly. Surface-level peacemaking results in something that looks like patience but functions like suppression. The result is a calm exterior that pushes down everything that’s never been allowed to be named.

Anger does not have to be dissolved before it is examined to show emotional maturity. Wisdom in handling emotions comes from understanding the difference between unrestrained anger and engaging with what has been building beneath the surface.

Christian counselors help individuals who have chosen suppression over engagement, or who have lived under the belief that burying difficult emotions was the faithful choice. The process of understanding repressed anger begins with realizing that it does not protect a person. It only delays what will need to be addressed at a greater cost.

Repressed Anger and the Body’s Honest Response

Emotional suppression and physical health have a well-documented connection, especially when it comes to anger. The body will respond over time when anger has been withheld rather than processed. It shows up in chronic muscle tension, recurring headaches, digestive difficulties, and disrupted sleep.

The body was not created to absorb what the mind refuses to examine. It will register what is carried and communicate it in ways that become increasingly hard to ignore as the body reveals hidden issues through outward symptoms.

God’s Word offers straightforward instruction to be slow to anger, but there is a deeper meaning in this instruction than first appears. When an individual is slowed to anger, they adopt a posture that reflects thoughtfulness, reflection, and a willingness to listen before reacting. This is the opposite of suppression, which bypasses reflection entirely and buries the emotion without engagement.

Christian counselors can help individuals focus on the intersection of faith and emotional health by helping clients distinguish between the responses of suppression and reflection. Suppression is not being slow to anger. It is avoidance. Whatever an individual consistently avoids will find other ways to make itself known, whether through physical symptoms, relationships, or behavior.

My dear brothers and sisters, take note of this: Everyone should be quick to listen, slow to speak and slow to become angry, because human anger does not produce the righteousness that God desires. – James 1:19-20, NIV

Finding Honest Ground Between Repressed Anger and Real Healing

When an individual moves away from the belief that their emotions are a spiritual problem and toward the understanding that the emotions carry spiritual information, they experience a meaningful shift. Anger often points to something real, even when it is buried. It indicates there was a boundary that was crossed, a wound that was minimized by others, or a loss that was never fully grieved.

Christian counselors recognize this shift and can help individuals name and grapple with the repressed anger that leads to an honest foundation where true healing can take place. Jesus never suggested that an offense be minimized or set aside.

He named it in a way that extends beyond interpersonal conflict. It reaches into the inner work of honestly acknowledging what has been dismissed or left untouched. Reconciliation requires honesty, whether it’s with oneself or with others.

The resolve to deal with what has been left unresolved isn’t a detour from faith, but rather wisdom in action. Many individuals find that their faith comes alive and is practical when they are honest about the repressed anger hidden beneath the surface.

Discover the Peace You Long For

People often smile when they don’t have the language or feel safe enough to do anything else. A smile is intended to be a reflection of wholeness that comes from the outward and inward life aligning. God’s Word does not ask people to perform emotionally. He invites them to genuine peace formed through honest engagement with Him in the reality of personal experience. This includes the parts that have been living quietly beneath the surface.

Jesus describes a peace that is not built on suppressing what is difficult, or on pretending that it’s not there. This peace comes to those who fully acknowledge what they carry. Those who are moving through the process of naming a long-buried emotion and following it to its source move into a place of honest healing. This isn’t a deficit of faith or the lack of it, but it can be how faith comes alive from the inside out.

Peace I leave with you; my peace I give you. I do not give to you as the world gives. Do not let your hearts be troubled and do not be afraid. – John 14:27, NIV

If you think you may struggle with repressed anger, you don’t have to suppress it any longer. You don’t have to navigate the journey of understanding that anger alone. Contact our office and speak with our reception team to make an appointment. They will connect you with support that will help you navigate mental health and faith honestly.
